title: Global aging can reshape security, labor, and health interests before U.S. policy treats it as a dedicated foreign-policy issue
source_unit: GAO-26-108732 literature review and expert interviews on global aging and U.S. foreign-policy interests, plus review of DOD, HHS, and State Department efforts
geography: Global demographic change and U.S. foreign-policy, security, economic, health, and humanitarian interests

observations.period: 2020-2050 demographic projection; GAO review published September 2026

denominator.unit: projected people age 60 and over worldwide in 2050

older_population_projection.value: global population age 60 and over is projected to rise from about 1.0 billion in 2020 to 2.1 billion in 2050

foreign_policy_channels.value: national security, economic competitiveness, and global health and humanitarian assistance
foreign_policy_channels.unit: three U.S. foreign-policy interest areas identified by GAO

ally_resource_tradeoff.value: aging allies may spend more on health care and have fewer resources available for defense

agency_response.value: DOD, HHS, and State address some implications indirectly through research, partner engagement, health or humanitarian assistance, and workforce preparation; no dedicated older-population foreign-assistance program was identified

geopolitical_endpoint.unit: changed defense budgets, alliance behavior, migration, labor competition, or U.S. strategic outcomes

observations.method: GAO conducted a literature review, interviewed selected academic and nongovernmental experts, reviewed DOD, HHS, and State documents and guidance, and interviewed agency officials.
observations.uncertainty: The report identifies plausible policy implications rather than estimating their size or causal timing. Expert and literature evidence does not establish country-specific defense tradeoffs, migration responses, alliance decisions, firm outcomes, or the effect of a dedicated U.S. program.
observations.subgroup: Older populations, U.S. allies and adversaries, labor markets, defense establishments, health systems, U.S. foreign-assistance agencies, and partner governments.
observations.counterinterpretation: Older populations may also contribute skills, care, savings, and social stability; defense spending can be shaped by threat, politics, and technology rather than aging alone. Countries may adapt through productivity, immigration, retirement reform, or other policies.

related_sources.claim: GAO full report and accessible version for global-aging implications and agency efforts.

boundary: This record maps a demographic trend to U.S. foreign-policy interest areas and records current agency attention. It does not estimate country-level causal effects, changed alliances, defense budgets, migration, labor markets, health outcomes, or U.S. strategic leverage.
